tone_statements.citation: Thang, Khoi Lam. 2001. A phonological reconstruction of Proto Chin. MA thesis, Payap University, Chiang Mai (xxi+173 pp.).
tone_statements.quote: 3.6.5 Tone In the current analysis, Kaang has five contrastive tones composed of three level tones and two contour tones. They are high tone //mid tone // low tone //rising tone //and falling tone //. Table 42 shows the tone distribution by syllable type in Kaang. [...] (p. 102:) This analysis shows that there are comparatively clearer tonal correspondences between Tedim, Mizo and Hakha. However, tone in Mara, Khumi and Kaang are split within the Patterns, tremendously complicated and without predictable environments.
tone_statements.locator: section 3.6.5 'Tone', p. 55 (Table 42 'Kaang tone distribution'); second sentence pair from section 4.6, p. 102 (after Table 114 'Chin tonal relationship')
tone_statements.n_tones: 5 (high, mid, low level; rising, falling contour)

sources.note: Stub; cites only Ethnologue (35,000 speakers, sub-groups Zo Kaang, Puei Kaang, Cum Kaang; lexical similarity with Welaung, Müün, Daai). Wikipedia 'Southern Kuki-Chin languages' cites Peterson 2017, VanBik 2009, So-Hartmann 1988, LSDO 2019.

sources.citation: So-Hartmann, Helga. 2009. A descriptive grammar of Daai Chin. STEDT Monograph 7. Berkeley: UC Berkeley.
sources.note: Describes Daai [dao], not Kaang. Mkaang appears only in history and subgrouping remarks (pp. 25-26: Ngmüün and Mkaang closest to Daai). Its stress discussion (weak presyllable + strong main syllable, iambic contour) concerns Daai and is not attributed to Kaang.

sources.citation: Thang, Khoi Lam. 2001. A phonological reconstruction of Proto Chin. MA thesis, Payap University, Chiang Mai (xxi+173 pp.).
sources.access_detail: a digital copy (available on request); access check: not located online or in the libraries checked
sources.note: Section 3.6 'Kaang' (printed pp. 52-55, pp. 73-76) is a 4-page synchronic sketch: syllable canon (C1)(C2)V1(V2)(C3)T, consonant and vowel inventories, segment distribution, and five contrastive tones (three level, two contour). The words 'stress' and 'accent' do not occur anywhere in the thesis. Kaang data = SIL MSEA 443-word wordlist collected by Seung Kim and Noel Mann (1999), retranscribed by the author ('The data for Kaang.. are from unpublished data collected by Seung Kim and Noel Mann').

tone.says: First-hand synchronic statement: Kaang syllable canon (C1)(C2)V1(V2)(C3)T with obligatory tone; five contrastive tones = three level (high, mid, low) + two contour (rising, falling); Table 42 gives tone distribution by syllable type (all five on smooth monophthong syllables; stopped -p/-t/-k syllables take rising, mid, falling, high; low tone only before -k; diphthong/long rhymes restricted). Ch. 4.6 (p. 102): Kaang reflexes of Luce's Chin tone patterns are 'split within the Patterns.. without…

sources.note: No thesis on Kaang. Chin theses present: Thang 2001 (Proto Chin), Mang 2006 (K'cho), Khar Thuan 2008 (Falam), Herr 2011 (Lemi), Naing Kheng 2017 (Mkuui Daai), Ngun Tin Par 2016 (Senthang).

sources.citation: ISO 639-3 Registration Authority. 2011. Change Request 2011-019 and New Code Request for [ckn] Chin, Kaang (adopted 2012-05-30). SIL International.
sources.note: No phonology. Alt names Kang, Kyuk-tu, Mkan, Mgan; 4-5 villages in Mindat Twp, <1,000 speakers; lacks the presyllables of Müün and Daai; c. 82% lexical similarity with Rawngtu; 'What written literature.. exist in this language?: none'; published sources: none listed; based on unpublished sociolinguistic research by Chin researchers in 2005 and 2011.

sources.citation: VanBik, Kenneth. 2009. Proto-Kuki-Chin: a reconstructed ancestor of the Kuki-Chin languages. STEDT Monograph 8. Berkeley.
sources.note: Comparative work; Kaang forms cited in cognate sets are taken from Thang 2001 (abbreviated PRPC/KLT). Notes that Thang's Kaang data 'faithfully represent tonal and vowel length distinctions' (p. 22). No Kaang stress statement.

sources.citation: So-Hartmann, Helga. 1988. Notes on the Southern Chin languages. Linguistics of the Tibeto-Burman Area 11(2): 98-119.
sources.note: Survey wordlists + phonetic correspondences. p. 98: 'Tone and/or register was not marked consistently in most of the lists, so I have not attempted to discuss it.' Mkaang: c. 1,200 speakers, three villages in Mindat Twp (p. 100); Mkaang wordlist informant from Hla Tui village (p. 108); Mkaang has lost prenasalization/preglottalization, has /f/, contrastive vowel length (p. 104). Nothing on stress.

Only references: So-Hartmann 2009 (pp. 25-26, subclassification) and Ethnologue (Eberhard et al. 2025). No descriptive reference listed; hh.bib held by the project links [ckn] only to Hartmann 1988 and Thang 2001.
